D5.scope: Models environment dynamics that support prediction, planning, and action; world models should not be equated with video generation alone.
D5.question: How can internal models reliably predict the consequences of actions in partially observed, changing environments?
D5.status: Model-based reinforcement learning and real-time interactive world generation have advanced considerably; long-horizon prediction, counterfactual actions, and real-world decision reliability remain unresolved.
methods: Compress high-dimensional observations into recursively updated latent states.
Use learned dynamics to plan, imagine trajectories, or optimize policies.
Predict future observations or environmental states conditioned on actions.
Incorporate physical constraints or structured priors to improve extrapolation.
timeline: A unified model-based RL configuration was evaluated across diverse control tasks.
An interactive real-time world generation system was demonstrated; the team also described limitations in interaction duration and control.
bottlenecks: Single-step prediction bias may compound across long rollouts; evaluation should consider both prediction horizon and planning utility.
Actions insufficiently covered by training policies may cause out-of-distribution dynamics errors.
Visual quality alone does not establish that learned transitions are valid for closed-loop control.
How different uncertainty sources should influence rollout length and behavioral risk remains an active research question.
links: Robotics: state estimation, planning, and control
Generative modeling: video simulation and action-conditioned generation
Bayesian ML: dynamic inference and uncertainty
opportunities: Connect model calibration errors to the planning horizon and test under distribution shift.
Empirical calibration does not directly establish formal safety guarantees.
Compare visual realism metrics, action prediction error, and closed-loop task utility.
True counterfactual outcomes may be unobservable in real environments.

E1.scope: Identify and validate computations inside neural networks. Many representative studies focus on language models, but the research questions are not limited to them.
E1.question: How can we show that a candidate neural circuit genuinely and consistently implements a computation, rather than simply correlating with its output?
E1.status: Feature dictionaries, surrogate models, and circuit-tracing tools are evolving rapidly; faithfulness, completeness, and cross-input generalization still lack unified validation.
methods: Use sparse decompositions to propose candidate intermediate features.
Trace candidate computational paths; surrogate-model graphs need not faithfully reproduce the original model.
Intervene on internal states and test whether proposed mechanisms predict behavior changes.
Assess the stability of explanations across inputs and model configurations.
timeline: Introduced circuit tracing and surrogate-model methods, while discussing faithfulness and reconstruction limitations.
Used attribution graphs to examine specific behaviors and illustrate both potential and limitations.
bottlenecks: A surrogate model’s attribution graph need not capture the computations the original model actually performs.
Analyses that freeze some attention patterns cannot explain how those patterns are formed.
Candidate features and graphs do not capture all of a model’s internal computation.
Showing an effect of an internal intervention does not eliminate alternative pathways or establish a complete mechanism.
links: Causal learning: intervention and mechanism identification
Deep learning architectures: internal computational structures to explain
opportunities: Separate discovery from confirmatory mechanism tests
Use independent tasks and held-out interventions to distinguish exploratory circuit discovery from confirmatory validation.
Sampling independence, intervention validity, and selection bias assumptions must be specified.
Report cross-input stability, reconstruction quality, and predicted intervention effects as distinct metrics.
No single metric can establish complete mechanism identification.

A5.scope: Use simulators or neural density estimators for repeated inference when likelihoods are intractable or posterior computation is costly; this is a subset of probabilistic ML.
A5.question: How can a limited simulation budget yield fast, diagnosable posterior approximations that are sensitive to model misspecification?
A5.status: ABC, NPE, NLE, and NRE now form established families of methods; expensive simulations, tail errors, posterior calibration, and real-world model misspecification remain active challenges.
methods: Use simulated data with distance functions or summary statistics for approximate inference.
Learn a likelihood approximation before performing inference.
Estimate density ratios for inference and hypothesis testing.
Repeatedly simulate and diagnose some calibration properties of an inference procedure.
timeline: Introduced benchmarks and metrics for comparing simulation-based inference methods.
Surveyed the statistical methods and applications of neural amortized inference.
The sbi documentation explains simulation-based calibration checks and their limitations.
bottlenecks: Calls to high-fidelity simulators can dominate training and diagnostic costs.
Globally amortized models may underperform on rare observations or complicated posterior regions.
Calibration is not guaranteed by a single diagnostic
SBC is an important diagnostic, but passing a single calibration check is not sufficient to establish posterior correctness.
An inference method that fits simulations may not be valid for reality when the simulator is wrong.
links: Scientific ML: complex simulators and inverse problems
Generative modeling: conditional density estimation and normalizing flows
opportunities: Use posterior diagnostics to reallocate simulation budgets; evaluate changes in coverage and tail accuracy.
Tuning and final evaluation should not rely on the same test data.
Investigate which statistics distinguish approximation error from errors in the simulator itself.
Simulations alone cannot establish real-world validity without further assumptions.
